rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
$$\%\text{yield}=\frac{\text{experimental (actual) yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}}\times100$$
$$\text{theoretical yield }(g)=n_{\text{limiting}}\times\frac{\nu_{\text{product}}}{\nu_{\text{limiting}}}\times M_{\text{product}}$$
$$\text{atom economy}=\frac{M_{\text{desired product}}}{\sum M_{\text{all reactants}}}\times100,\qquad \%\text{purity}=\frac{\text{mass of pure substance}}{\text{total mass of sample}}\times100$$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ A 100% yield means a pure product. ✅ Purity is a separate property; yields above 100% are the usual sign of an impure or wet product.  ·  ❌ Percentage yield is calculated from the reactant taken in excess. ✅ It is calculated from the limiting reactant, which fixes the theoretical yield.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Haber process: about 15% conversion per pass with recycling; the overall yield is raised by recycling unreacted N₂ and H₂.  ·  Typical undergraduate yields: aspirin 70–85%, soap 80–90%, esterification (equilibrium-limited) 60–70%.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** 100 g CaCO₃ gives 47.6 g CaO. Find the % yield. **Solution:** n(CaCO₃) = 1 mol → theoretical CaO = 56 g; % yield = 47.6/56 × 100 = 85%.  ·  **Problem:** 7.0 g of ethene (0.25 mol) is hydrated to give 9.2 g ethanol. Find the % yield. **Solution:** theoretical ethanol = 0.25 × 46 = 11.5 g; % yield = 9.2/11.5 × 100 = 80%.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: theoretical yield, experimental yield, % yield (within Stoichiometry).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ### 1. Meaning of the three quantities  ·  **Theoretical yield** is the maximum amount of product calculated from the balanced equation using the limiting reactant (assuming complete reaction and no losses). **Experimental (actual) yield** is the amount of pure product actually isolated in the experiment. **Percentage yield** compares them: $\%\text{yield}=\frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}}\times100$.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Atom economy of addition reactions is 100%, whereas substitution reactions lose part of the reactant mass as by-product.  ·  answer pattern for "Theoretical yield, experimental yield and % yield": define → method → result. Structure earns the marks on 6–10 mark questions.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: state + explain the main idea of "Theoretical yield, experimental yield and % yield" with one example.  ·  compare "Theoretical yield" with the related idea from a neighbouring unit.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Always quote the limiting reactant when explaining the theoretical yield — it is the only reactant that fixes it.  ·  Mention purity separately: yield ≠ purity, and >100% means an impure or wet sample.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 2. Why the actual yield is lower than the theoretical yield  ·  • The reaction is **incomplete** — the limiting reactant is not fully consumed in the time allowed.  ·  • The reaction is **reversible**, so it stops at an equilibrium position (this is exactly the case in the Haber process).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ The theoretical yield is what you actually get. ✅ It is the maximum possible amount; the actual yield is always lower for practical reasons.  ·  ❌ Yield and atom economy measure the same thing. ✅ Yield is about recovery of product; atom economy is about how much of the reactant mass ends up in the desired product.  ·  ❌ Yield can be predicted by stoichiometry alone. ✅ Stoichiometry gives only the theoretical maximum; the actual yield depends on kinetics, equilibrium and technique.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: For reversible processes (Haber, esterification) state that equilibrium limits the yield and recycling is used to improve the overall figure.  ·  List six reasons why the actual yield of a reaction is less than the theoretical yield.  ·  100 g of CaCO₃ on heating gives 47.6 g of CaO. Calculate the percentage yield.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: 0.25 mol of ethene is hydrated to ethanol but only 9.2 g is obtained. Calculate the percentage yield. (M(C₂H₅OH) = 46 g mol⁻¹)  ·  Explain why a student may report a yield greater than 100% and how the error can be corrected.  ·  Distinguish between percentage yield and atom economy and state the limitations of each.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: one worked example for "Theoretical yield, experimental yield and % yield" — check units / edge cases.  ·  recall card: definition → formula → limit → one error to avoid.  ·  State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: • **Side reactions** produce by-products (organic syntheses especially).  ·  • **Mechanical losses** during filtration, decantation, transfer, crystallisation, evaporation and drying, plus product remaining dissolved in the mother liquor (solubility loss).  ·  • Product may be **volatile, thermally unstable or hygroscopic**, and impurities may interfere with the reaction.
